title: EPIC Endgame Analysis!! | Belgrade Gambit | GM Naroditsky’s Theory Speed Run

moves.spoken: Black meets the king's pawn with the knight to c6 — a move that carries little independent value, meaning it usually just transposes into some other opening rather than standing on its own.

White keeps it simple with the knight to f3, sidestepping the need to learn a separate opening — because more often than not Black will follow up with e5 and everything transposes back to familiar ground.
And there it is, e5, and now White is right back in normal territory.
White reaches for the Belgrade Gambit — the knight to c3, inviting a sharp, ambitious fight. The trade-off is that this move order rules out the Vienna, but the gambit is the point.
White plays d4, offering the pawn. Black is very likely to grab it.
Black snaps it off — and now the true gambit begins.
This is the Belgrade Gambit: the knight leaps to d5, hitting the f6-knight and daring Black to sort out the complications.

Black chooses the knight to b4 — a move the books recommend and the engine likes, a sign the opponent knows the theory. But White has a quiet-looking weapon prepared here that breathes new life into the line.

White takes on f6 first. A warning against the queen recapture: do not grab the pawn on d4 afterwards — there is a simple tactic where Black plays the queen to d4 and the knight forks on c2, winning a piece.
Black recaptures with the queen.
So White chases the knight with a3 — and it has only one sensible square to drop back to.
Back it comes to c6. Now, this looks like a plain developing move, but there is subtlety behind it. White accepts that the pawn will only be won back in one specific case — if Black ever plays d6.
For now White just develops flexibly with the bishop to d3. The signal is clear: White is not chasing the pawn back — unless d6 appears, when the bishop jumps to b5.
And on cue: d6 is met by the bishop to b5, pinning the knight and setting up the recapture, ideally with a small edge.
Black finds the computer line, the bishop to g4 — a genuinely good, rarely-seen reply that only a well-prepared opponent knows.
White reclaims the pawn with the queen on d4.
Black offers the trade, and White is happy to head for an endgame — the sort of longer ending this run has not had much of.

The knight recaptures, and here is the honest assessment: the ending should be equal, but White has a touch more. Two reasons — slightly better central control, and, more importantly, the coming capture on c6 will damage Black's queenside pawns.
Black develops the bishop to d7. The key decision looms: when White captures on c6, which piece does it? Taking with the knight damages the structure, and that is the one worth aiming for.

White takes on c6 with the knight. It is less tempting because the recapture comes with tempo — but White does not want to hand over the bishop pair or uncontested control of the light squares. Keep the bishops on.
White develops the bishop to d3. Bishop to a6 was tempting, but after the rook drops back it would not be doing enough — and it would leave the e4-pawn, a central pillar, without support.
Remember that a piece can play a purely defensive role and still be a good piece. This bishop props up e4, and that is a job worth doing.
Black regroups the bishop to e7.
White develops the dark bishop to e3, leaning on the a7-pawn — and deliberately keeps the king's home undecided, waiting to see Black's plan before committing kingside, queenside, or staying central.

The bishop comes to f6, both developing and guarding b2. So White castles long, which also parks the rook on d1 where it x-rays the bishop. And a piece of realism: this ending will not be won quickly — Black is far too solid for a knockout. It is a slow, improving job.
The mindset matters as much as the moves — small improvements, patience, and being content to settle in for a long grind. The rook comes to b8.

Now a real decision on the queenside. The plan behind b3 and a4 is to provoke Black's a-pawn forward and then fix it on a dark square — because the whole endgame strategy is to manufacture long-term weaknesses to work against.
This is against the grain of instinct — in a fast game c3 is automatic — but going deeper, White wants to avoid creating weaknesses of his own. So b3 it is.
White plays a4, fixing the pawn. The queenside pawns stay healthy, and Black's are pinned down on colours White can target.
The reason to shun c3 here: it would leave the b2-pawn a long-term weakness, and Black could double rooks on the b-file to hammer it. Keep the structure clean.

Be alert to the standard freeing plan: Black would love to advance to c4, and if White ever has to take there, White inherits a weakness on a4 and the b-file cracks open. That is the break to watch for.
The bishop swings to c3.

White likes the idea of the bishop to c4 and the rook to d3, smoking the dark bishop out of c3. Why not simply trade with the bishop to d2? Because trading the dark bishops would make the a5-pawn untouchable — and you never want an unattackable weakness. Keep the dark bishop alive to hound a5.
White is genuinely happy with how this is going — real progress, and hard questions being posed to Black.

The rook lands on d3, and this is trickier still — it hands Black a chance to go wrong. If Black grabs on c4, White recaptures on c3 and wins the c6-pawn. And the key rule to remember: with opposite-coloured bishops and rooks still on, these positions are not the automatic draws people fear.
White has to take.
Recapturing gives Black doubled, isolated pawns — more targets. From here it has to be played very slowly.
The king steps to b2 to begin — patient, positional play. A lot of what follows is about where the pieces belong, not concrete variations.
Black pushes d5.
White answers with f3. This is exactly why the f-pawn was held back — to keep the option of defending the centre with f3 rather than rushing it forward.

That bishop on b4 is a nuisance, but c3 would be a bad idea — it softens b3 and kills the plan of the bishop to d2 hitting a5. So White switches targets: from the a5 weakness to Black's other one, the c6-pawn.

The idea is the bishop to d2, to trade the dark bishops so a rook can later land on c3 and rake the c-file. But first every piece needs to join in, so the second rook comes to d1 — a neutral, improving move that also discourages Black's freeing breaks with c5 or e5. White is slightly better, no more; with best play Black should hold, but it is unpleasant to defend.
Here is that plan again: the bishop to d2, so that if Black trades, the rook reroutes through c3 onto the prime c5 square.
The drawback is that after the trade Black's rook reaches the second rank — but that works out concretely for White. Pose the problem and see.
White takes the bishop.
Black recaptures, and the plan has landed — now White can go after the c6-pawn.

The rook heads to c3, aiming for c5, with the other rook to follow to c3 in turn — really leaning on Black's weaknesses. And no fear of the capture on c4: Black has three loose pawns to pick off and can grab only one in return.
The rook comes to c5, hitting another weakness on a5. Still only slightly better, but the balance is starting to tip.
Black cooperates, handing White everything he wants. The rook to a6 is another inaccuracy. Now the question is how to open a second front — because a single weakness is rarely enough.
So White opens lines with the capture on d5 — applying the principle of creating more weaknesses.

And breaks the chain with c4 — clearing the restricting pawn, opening prospects for the rooks, and eyeing the seventh rank. White is now much better, perhaps already technically winning — but rook endings are treacherous: one slip lets the defender get active.
Sensing it slipping, Black gives a pawn — which White gladly accepts.

A choice of two roads. The calm one is the rook takes on c6 with check, reaching a clean three-against-two that should be winning. The sharper one keeps both rooks on and goes hunting the g7-pawn — more ambitious, more calculation.
White takes the calmer route, the rook capturing on c6 with check.
Now the plan has two parts. First, watch the activity of every piece. The instinct is the king to c3 — but there is something even better to start with.

The rook to e1 first. If White leads with the king, Black slips a rook to e8 and forever threatens to infiltrate to e2. Lead with the rook, meet the rook, and only then march the king up — controlling every infiltration square.
Then phase two: begin advancing the kingside pawns, carefully and judiciously, with two aims — to create a passed pawn eventually, and to cramp Black's rook and soften his pawns.
White centralises the rook to e4 to start.
And there is a big moment brewing — the b4 break makes an outside passer. If White wants it, it has to be timed right, before Black locks the queenside with c5.

White judges the king to c3 fine here. Even if Black answers c5, the a5-pawn becomes a lasting weakness White can round up with the rook or approach with the king via b5 — so c5 only loosens the queenside further.
A frontal attack on White's kingside pawns leads nowhere — they are easily propped up with h4 or h3, and that is partly why the rook sits on e4 in the first place.
White locks Black's pawns with h4.

Now b4 — creating the passer. After the trade White recaptures with the king to stay maximally active, already close to pushing the a-pawn home. And there is a second idea on the other wing: if Black takes on h4, the rook recaptures and White is close to a second passer.
One passer already...
...and here is the second. Two connected threats on opposite wings — this has to be winning. The only question is technique.
The opponent is defending superbly — this is not simple to convert at all.
The idea now is to cut the king off with the rook, walling it away from the action.
Cut the king off — if Black holds even this, it is beautifully done.
White keeps torturing, but honestly this may well be a draw now — the defence has been excellent.
Still, the plan is to push with f4 and keep posing problems — this is genuinely hard to hold.
White plays f4, and there are tricky ideas lurking — notably that c5 for Black would actually lose.
And there it is: c5 walks into the check, the rook swings back, and White breaks through.

This resolves into a textbook Lucena — in fact Black's king is so completely cut off that it never even gets near the pawn. White simply escorts it home: bring the king to f8, push the pawn, and the checks from behind change nothing.
